stem: A client with cirrhotic ascites is being discharged on diuretic therapy. Which teaching about ongoing fluid-status and treatment monitoring is most appropriate?

options.A: Record body weight every day, track abdominal girth if instructed, and keep scheduled blood-test follow-up while taking diuretics so fluid response and treatment safety can be evaluated.
options.B: Use abdominal girth as the main daily measure and stop weighing once the waist measurement is stable, requesting blood tests only if visible swelling becomes worse.
options.C: Record daily weight but stop follow-up blood tests after the weight begins to fall, because weight loss confirms that the prescribed diuretic dose is being tolerated safely.
options.D: Rely on shortness of breath and ankle swelling to judge fluid accumulation and weigh only when these symptoms change instead of recording a daily weight trend.

rationale: AASLD outpatient cirrhosis guidance specifically includes monitoring daily weights for clients with ascites and adjusting diuretics according to tolerance and blood tests. Current StatPearls guidance states that clients with ascites treated with diuretics require ongoing monitoring of body weight, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and urinary sodium and identifies regular weight and abdominal-girth monitoring as useful for detecting worsening disease. Therefore A is correct. B makes abdominal girth a substitute for the specifically recommended daily weight trend and delays laboratory follow-up. C incorrectly treats falling weight as proof of diuretic safety despite the need for renal-function and electrolyte monitoring. D replaces direct serial fluid-status measurements with symptoms that may not appear early and abandons the recommended daily-weight trend.
educational_objective: For cirrhotic ascites treated with diuretics, use daily weight as a key longitudinal fluid-status measure, use abdominal girth as an adjunct when instructed, and continue laboratory monitoring for treatment tolerance and complications.
source_organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD); National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
source_document_title: Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis; Ascites — StatPearls
source_version_date: AASLD resource published February 15, 2024 and current on the AASLD site in 2026; StatPearls Ascites last updated November 30, 2025
source_locator: AASLD > Outpatient Cirrhosis Checklist > Ascites: discuss sodium restriction and monitoring daily weights; consider diuresis; adjust furosemide/spironolactone based on tolerance and blood tests. StatPearls Ascites > Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care: clients with ascites require long-term monitoring; body weight, electrolyte levels, BUN, creatinine, and urinary sodium should be monitored in clients treated with diuretics. > Deterrence and Patient Education: regular monitoring of weight and abdominal girth helps detect worsening disease early.
source_claim_supported: Daily weight is a key monitoring measure for cirrhotic ascites; abdominal girth can supplement trend monitoring, and diuretic therapy requires ongoing laboratory assessment of renal function and electrolytes rather than reliance on weight or symptoms alone.

supporting_sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
supporting_sources.locator: Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care: monitor body weight, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and urinary sodium in clients treated with diuretics. Deterrence and Patient Education: regular monitoring of weight and abdominal girth helps detect worsening disease early.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Weight and abdominal-girth trends support ascites monitoring, while renal-function and electrolyte monitoring remain necessary during diuretic therapy.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p. 42: perform focused assessments; recognize trends and changes in client condition and intervene as needed; monitor results of diagnostic testing and intervene as needed; evaluate client responses to procedures and treatments; educate the client about treatments and procedures.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — longitudinal fluid-status and laboratory monitoring during treatment of cirrhotic ascites
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four teaching statements to remove the absolute-word cue and uniquely-long keyed answer, narrowed the item to directly sourced monitoring behaviors, and remapped it to Reduction of Risk Potential because the item centers on trends, treatment response, and diagnostic laboratory monitoring.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Cirrhotic ascites — home fluid-status monitoring and diuretic safety follow-up
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies ascites plus diuretic therapy and asks one integrated monitoring-teaching question without inserting an unsupported numeric target.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects AASLD daily-weight guidance and current NCBI support for adjunct girth and laboratory monitoring; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — girth is useful as an adjunct, but it does not replace the AASLD-recommended daily weight trend or routine laboratory follow-up during diuretic treatment.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — daily weight is appropriate, but weight loss alone cannot establish renal/electrolyte safety or justify stopping follow-up blood testing.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — respiratory or edema symptoms can be clinically relevant, but symptom-triggered weighing does not replace recommended serial weight monitoring.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that preserves daily weight monitoring while correctly retaining adjunct assessment and treatment-safety follow-up.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B substitutes girth for weight and delays labs, C abandons safety monitoring, and D abandons longitudinal weight trends.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — the keyed response is comparable in length and complexity to the distractors, and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Reduction of Risk Potential directly includes focused assessment, trend recognition, diagnostic-test monitoring, treatment-response evaluation, and client education.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether abdominal girth could reasonably serve as the primary home measure or falling weight could be sufficient to judge treatment response; AASLD specifically calls for daily weights and blood-test-guided diuretic adjustment, while NCBI treats girth as additional monitoring and retains renal/electrolyte surveillance, leaving A uniquely best.
